To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

electrochemical aptamer sensors can be used to measure drugs continuously in the bloodstream of awake, ambulatory rodents for up to 4 h, achieving clinically relevant detection limits, high temporal resolution, and high precision.

E-AB sensors can be used to perform continuous, real-time measurements of drugs in the blood of living animals for extended periods of time (e.g., 4 hours), with high (3 s or better) temporal resolution.
we have demonstrated for the first time the ability to use E-AB sensors for the continuous, real-time monitoring of drugs directly in the bloodstream of awake, ambulatory subjects.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of electrochemical sensors for real-time, multiday molecular measurements in the bloodstream of awake, ambulatory subjects.
the development of electrochemical aptamers (E-ABs) and their use in real-time measurements.
the development of electrochemical aptamers (E-ABs), which are aptamers that can be reversibly switched between an inactive and active state by application of an electric potential (Figure 1).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have demonstrated the feasibility of a new technology for the real-time, multiday, in vivo tracking of small molecules in the bloodstream of living subjects.

we have demonstrated the ability of electrochemically based aptamer-based (EBAB) sensors to perform the real-time, multihar measurement of small molecules in the bloodstream of living animals, even awake and ambulatory rats, and that the approach could be a useful new tool in physiology, pharmacokinetic, and toxicological studies.
we have demonstrated the feasibility of performing multihour, in vivo molecular measurements in living, ambulatory animals using E-AB sensors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the E-AB sensor technology is capable of performing real-time, high-resolution molecular measurements in the body of living subjects.

we have developed an approach for continuous, real-time monitoring of drugs in the bloodstream that could provide a window into physiology, pharmacokinetic, and toxicological studies, and could enable the development of personalized drug delivery systems and other applications in personalized medicine.

we have demonstrated the ability of electrochemically based aptamer sensors to provide continuous, real-time measurements of arbitrary molecules directly in the bloodstream of living animals, even awake, ambulating rats.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have shown that the use of E-AB sensors in living animals is not only feasible but also provides a powerful new tool for the study of physiology.
E-AB sensors can support the continuous, real-time measurement in vivo of arbitrary molecules at clinically relevant detection levels.

we now have a new technology capable of performing the real-time, multiday, continuous measurement of arbitrary molecules in the body, a capability that could have profound impact in a broad range of applications in biology and medicine.
